questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which deep neck infection presents with bilateral submandibular and submental swelling with a raised woody tongue and airway threat?
questions.concept: It usually arises from a lower molar tooth, involves the submandibular, submental and sublingual spaces, and airway management with drainage and antibiotics takes precedence over imaging.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which space infection causes trismus with medial displacement of the tonsil and a risk of carotid sheath involvement?
questions.concept: Because the space contains the carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX to XII, complications include internal jugular thrombosis, carotid erosion and cranial neuropathy.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which foreign body site is most common in a child who inhales a peanut, and why?
options: The right main bronchus, because it is wider, shorter and more vertical
questions.concept: Unilateral wheeze with reduced air entry and a normal radiograph does not exclude it, so a strong history warrants rigid bronchoscopy.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which radiological sign indicates a retropharyngeal abscess in a child?
options: Widening of the prevertebral soft tissue shadow on a lateral neck radiograph
questions.concept: The steeple sign indicates croup and the thumb sign epiglottitis, and contrast computed tomography distinguishes cellulitis from a drainable collection.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which complication of a deep neck infection presents with rigors, septic pulmonary emboli and internal jugular vein thrombosis?
options: Lemierre syndrome, usually due to Fusobacterium necrophorum
questions.concept: It follows oropharyngeal infection in a young adult, is diagnosed by contrast imaging of the neck and chest, and is treated with prolonged antibiotics with anticoagulation in selected cases.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which oesophageal site is the commonest for a swallowed coin to lodge in a child?
options: At the cricopharyngeus, the narrowest point about 15 cm from the incisors
At the left main bronchus crossing
questions.concept: A coin lodged in the oesophagus appears as a full circle on an anteroposterior film whereas one in the trachea appears edge-on, which is a useful radiological distinction.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Which button battery ingestion feature makes it a surgical emergency rather than an observed foreign body?
options: Lodgement in the oesophagus, because electrolytic injury causes mucosal necrosis and perforation within hours
questions.concept: The double-ring or halo sign on radiograph identifies it, and endoscopic removal within 2 hours is the aim because delay leads to tracheo-oesophageal or aorto-oesophageal fistula.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Why does mediastinitis complicate a deep neck infection, and along which plane does it spread?
options: Infection tracks down the retropharyngeal and danger space to the posterior mediastinum, which is continuous with the neck
It spreads through the bloodstream only
It spreads via lymphatics to the mediastinum
It cannot spread below the clavicle
questions.concept: Because the danger space between the alar and prevertebral fascia extends to the diaphragm, descending necrotising mediastinitis carries a high mortality and requires aggressive thoracic drainage.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Why is a laryngeal foreign body more immediately life threatening than a bronchial one?
options: It obstructs the narrowest part of the airway completely and provokes laryngospasm, whereas a bronchial foreign body leaves one lung ventilated
questions.concept: This explains why a complete laryngeal obstruction demands immediate back blows or abdominal thrusts, and cricothyroidotomy if these fail, rather than transfer for endoscopy.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Deep Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which salivary gland most often forms calculi, and why?
options: The submandibular gland, because its secretion is more mucinous and alkaline and the duct runs upward against gravity
questions.concept: Colicky swelling of the gland at mealtimes is characteristic, and most stones are radio-opaque so a plain film or ultrasound identifies them.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which viral infection causes bilateral painful parotid swelling with a risk of orchitis and deafness?
questions.concept: Bilateral involvement distinguishes it from suppurative parotitis, which is unilateral with pus expressible from the duct and occurs in dehydrated or debilitated patients.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which premalignant oral lesion carries a higher risk of malignant transformation than leukoplakia?
questions.concept: A red velvety patch that cannot be scraped off has a transformation risk of up to about 30 percent, which is far higher than white patches, so early biopsy is essential.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which condition presents with progressive trismus, blanching of the oral mucosa and fibrous bands in a habitual areca nut chewer?
questions.concept: It is potentially malignant, largely irreversible, and management combines habit cessation with intralesional steroid, physiotherapy and surgery for severe trismus, along with surveillance for carcinoma.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which sign indicates that a parotid mass is malignant rather than benign?
options: Facial nerve palsy, fixity to skin or deep tissue, pain or cervical lymphadenopathy
questions.concept: Fine needle aspiration and imaging assist, but any facial weakness with a parotid mass is regarded as strongly suggestive of malignancy and changes the surgical plan.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which surgical procedure is standard for a benign tumour of the superficial lobe of the parotid?
options: Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation
questions.concept: Enucleation leaves pseudopodia behind and causes recurrence in pleomorphic adenoma, and Frey syndrome of gustatory sweating is a recognised late complication of the operation.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which condition causes a dry mouth and dry eyes with bilateral parotid enlargement and a risk of lymphoma?
questions.concept: Antibodies to Ro and La with a labial gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis support it, and the risk of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma justifies long-term surveillance.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Why does a squamous carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue present later and with a worse prognosis than one of the anterior two thirds?
options: It is less visible and less painful early, and the region has rich bilateral lymphatic drainage so nodal spread occurs early
It is always detected on routine examination
questions.concept: This is why persistent unilateral otalgia, referred through the glossopharyngeal nerve, or a neck node without an obvious primary should prompt examination of the base of the tongue.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Why is a persistent unilateral serous otitis media in an adult from a high-incidence region an indication for nasopharyngeal biopsy?
options: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma can obstruct the eustachian tube and presents with a neck node and unilateral effusion before any nasal symptom
Effusions in adults are always benign
The tube is never obstructed by tumour
questions.concept: Its association with Epstein-Barr virus, salted fish consumption and genetic susceptibility, and its radiosensitivity, make early diagnosis particularly worthwhile.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oral Cavity and Salivary Glands

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Otitis media, CSOM, hearing loss
questions.stem: Which organism most commonly causes acute suppurative otitis media in a child?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae, followed by Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis
questions.concept: Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus dominate chronic suppurative disease instead, which is why the antibiotic choice differs between acute and chronic infection.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Middle Ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Otitis media, CSOM, hearing loss
questions.stem: Which stage of acute suppurative otitis media is characterised by relief of pain with the onset of discharge?
options: The stage of suppuration with perforation
questions.concept: The bulging drum ruptures, releasing the pressure, and myringotomy achieves the same relief in a controlled way while preserving the drum.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Middle Ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Otitis media, CSOM, hearing loss
questions.stem: Which finding indicates the need for myringotomy in acute otitis media?
options: A severely bulging drum with persistent severe pain, or a complication such as facial palsy
questions.concept: An incision in the antero-inferior quadrant avoids the ossicles and the round window niche, and it heals without permanent perforation.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Middle Ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Otitis media, CSOM, hearing loss
questions.stem: Which type of hearing loss follows chronic suppurative otitis media with extensive ossicular erosion, and what is the audiometric pattern?
options: Conductive loss with a large air-bone gap approaching 60 dB
Mixed loss with a small gap
questions.concept: A gap larger than the maximum possible for a conductive lesion indicates a coexisting sensorineural component from toxin diffusion through the round window.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Middle Ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Otitis media, CSOM, hearing loss
questions.stem: Which surgical procedure removes disease while preserving the posterior canal wall in cholesteatoma?
options: Canal wall up (intact canal wall) mastoidectomy, which requires careful follow-up for residual disease
questions.concept: Canal wall down procedures give better disease clearance but leave a cavity requiring lifelong care, so the choice balances the risk of residual disease against cavity problems.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Middle Ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Otitis media, CSOM, hearing loss
questions.stem: Why is a cholesteatoma described as skin in the wrong place rather than as a tumour?
options: It is a sac of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear whose expansion and enzymatic activity erode bone, though it is not neoplastic
It is a benign neoplasm of squamous cells
questions.concept: The name is a historical misnomer, and its danger comes from bone erosion producing intracranial and labyrinthine complications rather than from malignant potential.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Middle Ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which vessel is the commonest source of severe posterior epistaxis in an older hypertensive patient?
options: The sphenopalatine artery, in Woodruff plexus
questions.concept: Anterior bleeding from Little area is commoner overall and easier to control, whereas posterior bleeding needs posterior packing, endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which first-aid measure is correct for anterior epistaxis?
options: Firm pinching of the cartilaginous part of the nose with the patient sitting and leaning forward
Pinching the bony bridge lying supine
questions.concept: Leaning forward prevents swallowing blood, which causes vomiting and obscures ongoing loss, and topical vasoconstrictor with cautery follows if pressure fails.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which paranasal sinus is most often involved in sinusitis, and why?
options: The maxillary sinus, because its ostium lies high on the medial wall so gravity-dependent drainage is poor
The frontal sinus, because it is largest
The sphenoid sinus, because it is deepest
The ethmoid sinus, because it has no ostium
questions.concept: Pain that worsens on stooping, with tenderness over the cheek and postnasal discharge, is characteristic, and dental infection is a recognised unilateral cause.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which complication of ethmoidal sinusitis is commonest in a child, and how is it staged?
options: Orbital cellulitis, staged by the Chandler classification from preseptal cellulitis to cavernous sinus thrombosis
questions.concept: The thin lamina papyracea separates the ethmoids from the orbit, and proptosis, reduced eye movement or visual change indicate a postseptal collection requiring imaging and drainage.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which imaging is used to assess chronic sinusitis before endoscopic sinus surgery?
options: Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses in the coronal plane
questions.concept: Computed tomography maps the bony anatomy including the ethmoid roof, orbital wall and optic nerve, whereas magnetic resonance is reserved for suspected intracranial or fungal extension.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which condition causes a mucosal ulcer and septal perforation with a history of cocaine use or previous surgery?
options: Septal perforation from ischaemic necrosis of cartilage
questions.concept: Perforation causes whistling, crusting and epistaxis, and other causes include trauma, granulomatous disease, tuberculosis and prolonged topical steroid use with poor technique.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Which feature of a deviated nasal septum makes surgical correction appropriate rather than observation?
options: Symptomatic obstruction, recurrent sinusitis or epistaxis attributable to the deviation
Cosmetic concern alone in a child
Presence of a spur without symptoms
questions.concept: Septoplasty preserves and repositions cartilage rather than resecting it as in the older submucous resection, which reduces the risk of saddle deformity and septal perforation.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Why is a young adult with recurrent severe epistaxis and telangiectasia on the lips investigated for a systemic disorder?
options: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia can involve pulmonary and cerebral arteriovenous malformations that carry serious risk
Epistaxis in youth is never significant
questions.concept: The autosomal dominant condition requires screening of the lungs and brain and of first-degree relatives, so recognising the pattern in the nose has consequences well beyond the nose.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Sinusitis, epistaxis, DNS
questions.stem: Why is a persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with bleeding in an adult treated as suspicious even when examination looks benign?
options: Sinonasal malignancy and inverted papilloma present exactly this way and are easily missed without endoscopy and imaging
questions.concept: The maxillary antrum is the commonest site, and by the time facial swelling, epiphora, loose teeth or diplopia appear the disease is already advanced.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Nose and Sinuses

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Which indication for tonsillectomy is supported by the strongest evidence?
options: Recurrent documented tonsillitis meeting frequency criteria, or obstructive sleep-disordered breathing
questions.concept: Sleep-disordered breathing with adenotonsillar hypertrophy in a child is now the commonest indication, and unilateral enlargement in an adult raises the question of lymphoma or carcinoma.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Which complication of tonsillectomy occurs within the first 24 hours and is usually due to inadequate haemostasis?
options: Primary or reactionary haemorrhage, requiring return to theatre
questions.concept: Secondary haemorrhage occurs at 5 to 10 days from slough separation with infection and is usually managed with antibiotics and observation, though it can be severe.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Which staging feature of laryngeal carcinoma most strongly influences the decision between larynx preservation and total laryngectomy?
options: Cartilage invasion and involvement of the pre-epiglottic or paraglottic space with cord fixation
questions.concept: Early tumours are treated by radiotherapy or transoral laser surgery with excellent voice preservation, whereas extensive cartilage invasion predicts poor response to organ preservation.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Which finding indicates a peritonsillar abscess rather than acute tonsillitis?
options: Unilateral severe pain with trismus, a muffled voice, uvular deviation and a bulging soft palate
questions.concept: Aspiration or incision and drainage with antibiotics is the treatment, and interval tonsillectomy is considered because of the recurrence risk.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Which condition must be excluded before tonsillectomy in a child with a bifid uvula or submucous cleft palate?
options: Velopharyngeal insufficiency, which tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy could unmask
questions.concept: Removing the adenoid in such a child can produce hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation, so a partial or superior adenoidectomy is used if surgery is needed at all.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Which route of spread makes supraglottic carcinoma present with nodal disease earlier than glottic carcinoma?
options: Rich bilateral lymphatic drainage of the supraglottis, in contrast to the sparse lymphatics of the true cords
questions.concept: This anatomical difference explains both the earlier nodal disease and the need to treat the neck electively in supraglottic tumours even when it appears clinically negative.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Tonsillitis, carcinoma larynx
questions.stem: Why does referred otalgia occur in carcinoma of the larynx or base of tongue?
options: Shared sensory innervation through the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves refers pain to the ear via Arnold and Jacobson nerves
Direct tumour extension to the ear
questions.concept: This is why a patient with persistent unilateral otalgia and a normal ear examination must have the larynx and pharynx examined carefully.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Diseases of Oropharynx and Larynx

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which condition causes brief episodic vertigo lasting under a minute triggered by head position change, with a positive Dix-Hallpike test?
options: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo from otolith debris in the posterior canal
questions.concept: The Epley repositioning manoeuvre resolves most cases, and the characteristic geotropic torsional nystagmus with latency and fatigability confirms the diagnosis.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which tetrad characterises Meniere disease?
options: Episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness
Brief positional vertigo with normal hearing
Progressive hearing loss with no vertigo
questions.concept: Endolymphatic hydrops is the pathological basis, low frequencies are affected first, and management combines salt restriction with betahistine and diuretics, escalating to intratympanic therapy.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which condition causes acute severe vertigo lasting days with normal hearing after a viral illness?
questions.concept: Labyrinthitis includes hearing loss because the cochlea is involved, and vestibular rehabilitation with a short course of vestibular sedative is the approach, avoiding prolonged suppressant use which delays compensation.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a central from a peripheral cause of vertigo?
options: Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus that is not suppressed by fixation, with other brainstem or cerebellar signs
Horizontal nystagmus with a fast phase away from the lesion
questions.concept: The HINTS examination with head impulse, nystagmus and test of skew is more sensitive than early imaging for posterior circulation stroke in acute continuous vertigo.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which grading system describes the severity of facial nerve palsy?
options: House-Brackmann grading from I to VI
questions.concept: Documenting the grade at presentation and during recovery is what allows treatment decisions and prognostication, and electroneuronography adds prognostic information in complete palsy.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which treatment improves outcome in Bell palsy, and when must it be started?
options: Oral corticosteroids started within 72 hours of onset
questions.concept: Antivirals add little except possibly in severe palsy, and eye care with lubricants and taping to prevent exposure keratopathy is as important as the drug treatment.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which condition causes facial palsy with vesicles in the external auditory canal and severe otalgia?
options: Ramsay Hunt syndrome from varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion
Acute otitis media with facial palsy
questions.concept: It has a poorer prognosis than Bell palsy, and combined aciclovir with corticosteroid started early improves the chance of complete recovery.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Which site of facial nerve lesion is indicated by palsy with loss of taste, reduced lacrimation and hyperacusis?
options: A lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion, above the greater petrosal branch
A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen
A lesion in the parotid gland
A lesion of the facial nucleus
questions.concept: Topodiagnostic testing follows the branches in order, with the nerve to stapedius affecting the acoustic reflex and the chorda tympani affecting taste and submandibular secretion.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Vertigo, Meniere's disease & facial nerve palsy
questions.stem: Why does a vestibular schwannoma cause progressive unilateral hearing loss with disproportionate tinnitus but relatively little vertigo?
options: Slow growth allows central vestibular compensation, whereas cochlear nerve compression progressively impairs hearing
It does not involve the vestibular nerve
It grows too fast for compensation
questions.concept: Asymmetric sensorineural loss with poor speech discrimination is the classic presentation, and magnetic resonance imaging of the internal auditory meatus is the investigation of choice.
questions.reference: Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 8e, Ch. Vertigo and Facial Nerve
